opus-5.5.text:
The web was built for human eyes. Every website is designed so that a person can look at the screen and figure out what to do: where the search box is, which button checks out, what the menu contains. That visual layer is the one thing that's consistent across millions of sites, even though what's underneath varies enormously.

If you build an agent that relies only on the underlying structure, like the HTML, the DOM, or accessibility trees, you run into trouble quickly. Every site is implemented differently. Some have clean, semantic markup, and a lot don't. You get dynamically rendered content, canvas elements, iframes, custom components that are just nested divs with no meaningful labels. The DOM can also be enormous, tens of thousands of tokens of noise, when what matters is a handful of elements. So a text-only agent ends up brittle. It works well on the sites it was tuned for and falls apart on the long tail.

Vision gives you a kind of universal interface. If the agent can see the page the way a person does, it can reason about layout, about visual hierarchy, about what looks clickable, about the fact that a form appeared after it pressed something. Those cues carry a lot of meaning that never appears cleanly in the markup. And because humans already know how to use websites they've never seen before, mostly from visual conventions, an agent that perceives things similarly can generalize in the same way.

In practice I don't think it's vision versus structure. The strongest approach combines them. You use the screenshot to understand what's going on and the structured information when it's available to act precisely. But if the goal is one agent that works across many websites rather than a custom integration for each, vision is what makes that generalization possible. It's the common denominator.

r001.rationale: The response says screenshots provide a common visual interface across sites and that vision makes generalization possible, while DOM-only agents are brittle.

r002.rationale: It notes that site implementations and markup vary, but does not clearly explain that extracting DOM element information requires website-specific parsing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is: the web was built for humans, and humans consume it visually. Every website is designed so that a person looking at a screen can figure out what to do. So if you want one agent that generalizes across many websites rather than something hand-tuned for each one, the most universal interface you have is the rendered page itself.

The alternative is to work from the DOM or the HTML, and that works fine when you're building for a handful of sites. But the DOM is incredibly messy and inconsistent. Two sites that look nearly identical to a user can have completely different underlying structure. There are nested divs, dynamically generated class names, elements that exist in the HTML but aren't actually visible, and increasingly things rendered in canvas or through frameworks where the text representation doesn't tell you much. If your agent's understanding of a page depends on parsing all of that, it becomes brittle. It breaks when a site redesigns, and it doesn't transfer to the next site.

Vision gives you something closer to what a human sees. A button looks like a button. A form looks like a form. Spatial layout carries meaning: things that are grouped together visually usually belong together semantically, and that's a signal the DOM often obscures. So a model that perceives the page as pixels is learning the same affordances that humans rely on, which is exactly the thing that's consistent across websites, because designers are all optimizing for the same human eyes.

There's also a practical point about actions. Humans interact with the web through clicks, scrolls, and typing at screen locations. If your agent perceives visually and acts in that same space, you don't need per-site integrations or APIs. You get one interface for everything.

That said, I don't think it's vision instead of everything else. Text and accessibility trees are useful, and the strongest systems combine them. But if you're asking what gives you the broadest generalization, it's the ability to look at the screen and understand it, because that's the one thing every website shares.

r001.rationale: The response says the rendered page is the most universal interface for an agent that generalizes across websites, contrasting it with parsing the DOM.

r002.rationale: It explains that DOM structures are messy and inconsistent across sites, so an agent relying on parsing them becomes brittle and needs per-site handling.

astra-6.text:
I think vision gives us a common interface across websites. If you or I go to a website we’ve never seen before, we can look at the page, understand roughly how it’s organized, find a search box or a button, and figure out what to do. We don’t need to understand how that particular website was implemented.

For an agent, the underlying structure can vary quite a bit from one website to another, even when they support very similar tasks. Being able to reason about what’s rendered on the screen gives the agent a way to generalize across those differences. It can connect an instruction like “find this product” to the search box it sees, take an action, and then look at the result to decide what to do next.

That doesn’t mean vision has to be the only input. The page structure can be useful too. But vision provides a shared foundation for interacting with interfaces that were designed for people.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning about what is rendered on screen helps an agent generalize across websites with varying underlying structures, conveying the role of visual page input over dependence on site-specific structure.

r002.rationale: It notes that website structure varies, but does not explain that extracting element information from the DOM requires website-specific parsing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision gives you a common interface across websites. Underneath, every website can be implemented differently—the DOM structure, the names of elements, all of that can vary. But as humans, we can go to a website we’ve never seen before, look at it, and usually figure out where to click or where to type. We don’t need access to its underlying code.

So if you want a single agent that can operate across many websites, being able to understand what’s on the screen is a powerful capability. It can connect an instruction like “find this item and add it to my cart” to the buttons, text fields, and other elements it sees. Vision isn’t necessarily the only input you’d want, but it gives the agent a shared way of interacting with environments that otherwise look very different under the hood.

r001.rationale: It presents visual screen understanding as a shared way for one agent to work across sites whose DOMs differ, without needing their underlying code.

r002.rationale: It says DOM structures and element names vary, but does not explain that extracting element information requires website-specific parsing.
